title: Best Weighted Sum Over All Rotations
statement:
You get an integer array nums of length n. The weighted sum of an arrangement a is 0·a[0] + 1·a[1] + … + (n − 1)·a[n − 1]: each value times its index.

Consider all n rotations of nums (rotating right by 0, 1, …, n − 1 steps). Return the largest weighted sum among them.

examples.why: [-3, -1] scores −1 and [-1, -3] scores −3. The answer can be negative, so do not start the maximum at 0.
A single value always sits at index 0.

hints: Computing each rotation's sum from scratch is O(n) per rotation. How does the sum change from one rotation to the next?
Rotating right by one adds 1 to every index except the last value's, which drops from n − 1 to 0.
So F(k) = F(k − 1) + sum(nums) − n · (the value that just wrapped to the front).

explain.intuition:
Each rotation is a small change from the previous one. Rotate right by one step: every value moves one index up, adding the value once more to the total, so the sum grows by S = sum(nums). Except the value that was last: it was counted n − 1 times and now sits at index 0. Taking that into account, F(k) = F(k − 1) + S − n · v, where v is the value that wrapped to the front.

The value that wraps on step k is nums[n − k]. Compute F(0) directly, then update in O(1) per rotation.
steps: Compute S = sum(nums) and F = Σ i · nums[i].
For k from 1 to n − 1: F += S − n · nums[n − k] and update best.
pitfalls: Starting best at 0. With all negative values every rotation is negative.
Using the wrong wrapped value: rotating right moves nums[n − k] to the front, not nums[k − 1].
Building each rotated array: O(n²) time and lots of copying.

solutions.title: Score every rotation directly
solutions.idea: For each k, compute the weighted sum by reading nums with an offset.

solutions.title: One-step recurrence
solutions.idea: Each right rotation adds sum(nums) and subtracts n times the value that wrapped to the front.

followups: Return the rotation count k that gives the best sum, breaking ties by the smallest k.
The weights are now arbitrary w[i] instead of i. Is there still a fast method? (Hint: convolution.)
